design_principles.principle: Make the two test families feel different
design_principles.app_approach: Cross-sectional tests (FM/FF92) live in scatter-of-returns-on-betas land; time-series tests (GRS) live in Sharpe-geometry land. Separate visual grammars, one punchline: both ask if some portfolio is MV-efficient.

design_principles.principle: Run Fama–MacBeth, don't read about it
design_principles.app_approach: A month-by-month simulator: watch each cross-sectional slope wobble, watch the histogram of slopes build, and see why the time-series s.e. is the honest one.
Crank the beta-measurement noise and watch the fitted slope collapse toward zero — then click 'form portfolios' and watch it recover.
FF92 Table III and the FF93 5×5 grids ship with the actual published numbers; students toggle specifications and watch alphas shrink.
Drag the market inside the frontier; the Sharpe gap and the F-statistic update live. Rejecting the CAPM = measuring a distance.

slides.title: Two Lines, One Model: CML vs SML
slides.content_summary: CAPM recap (Sharpe–Lintner + Black). CML in σ-space holds only efficient portfolios; SML in β-space holds ALL assets. Four testable implications; time-series (α=0) vs cross-sectional (β suffices) tests.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Security 1 has the same expected return as the tangency but far more σ. Why isn't that a violation?'

slides.title: Only Covariance Gets Paid
slides.content_summary: σi² = βi²σM² + σ²(εi). Drag β and idiosyncratic noise; watch total risk split. Huge-variance, zero-beta asset earns rf — diversification washes the noise out.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Set β=0 and σε huge. Why does the CAPM still say E[r]=rf?'

slides.title: Run Fama–MacBeth Month by Month
slides.content_summary: Two passes: TS regression per asset for betas; then one cross-section per month. Simulator: step through months, watch each slope; histogram builds; FM mean and s.e. = time-series s.e. of the slopes (honest because common shocks land in slope variation).
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why is one big regression of average returns on betas the same point estimate but the WRONG t-stat?'

slides.title: The Noisy Beta Problem
slides.content_summary: EIV: β̂=β+e ⟹ γ̂2 = Cov(r,β)/(Var(β)+Var(e)) — attenuation. Noise dial shrinks the fitted slope; 'form portfolios' button diversifies e away (at the cost of β spread). Plus microstructure and the regression phenomenon in Lux's pocket.

slides.title: Your Turn: How Much Does Noise Bite?

problem_spec.scenario: True premium slope 0.60%/mo; cross-sectional Var(β)=0.09; beta-estimation noise Var(e)=0.09.

slides.title: FF92: Beta Is Dead
slides.content_summary: The double-sort design (100 size×β portfolios, post-ranking betas) creates β variation independent of size. Table I: returns fall with size, flat in β. Table III (real numbers): β alone 0.15 (t 0.46); ln(ME) −0.15 (−2.58); ln(BE/ME) 0.50 (5.71); joint −0.11/0.35 (−1.99/4.44). Spec picker with published values.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'BE/ME kills leverage and size kills E/P. What does 'kills' mean in a regression?'

slides.title: One Hypothesis to Rule Them All
slides.content_summary: Roll: the CAPM's only testable claim is that M is MV-efficient — betas against any ex-post efficient portfolio fit by construction; proxies make rejection ambiguous (Stambaugh: not fatal; Kandel–Stambaugh: Corr>0.70 suffices). GRS operationalizes exactly this: joint α=0 with J1 = [(T−N−1)/N]·α̂'Σ̂⁻¹α̂/(1+θ̂m²) ~ F(N,T−N−1).

slides.title: The Sharpe-Gap Picture
slides.content_summary: α'Σ⁻¹α = θq²−θm². Drag M off the frontier; rays from the origin show both Sharpes at σ=1; hypotenuse ratio gives J1 live for chosen T and N. Rejection = distance.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Double T with the same Sharpe gap. Why does J1 double — what did more months buy you?'

slides.title: Your Turn: Compute a GRS Statistic

problem_spec.scenario: Monthly data: T=111, N=10 test assets. In-sample tangency Sharpe θq=0.25; market Sharpe θm=0.15 (monthly units).
problem_spec.verification: θq²=0.0625, θm²=0.0225, gap=0.04. (T−N−1)/N = 100/10 = 10. J1 = 10·0.04/1.0225 = 0.3912. F(10,100) 5% critical ≈ 1.93 ⟹ FAIL to reject despite the seemingly large Sharpe improvement — 111 months is not much evidence.

slides.title: Building SMB and HML
slides.content_summary: The 2×3 sort (NYSE median size × 30/70 BE/ME) into SL..BH; SMB = ⅓(S row) − ⅓(B row); HML = ½(H column) − ½(L column); ≈orthogonal by construction. Plus TERM and DEF, and why bonds join the test assets. Economic motivation (FF95 distress/earnings persistence).
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why NYSE breakpoints? What would happen with all-market breakpoints?'

slides.title: The 5×5 Grid, With Real Numbers
slides.content_summary: Heatmap of the 25 size×BE/ME portfolios with FF93's actual published numbers. Toggle: average excess returns (Table 1), CAPM alphas (9a-ii), three-factor alphas (9a-iv), HML loadings (Table 6). Watch the value column's alphas vanish under three factors — except the stubborn small-growth corner. GRS row: 2.09/1.91/1.78/1.56/1.66.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Which corner does the 3-factor model still miss, and what's the sign of its alpha?' (small-growth, −0.34, t=−3.16)

slides.title: Your Turn: Price a Stock with Three Factors

problem_spec.scenario: Loadings b=1.0, s=0.6, h=0.4. Annual premia: market 6%, SMB 2.5%, HML 4%.

slides.title: What Rejecting the CAPM Buys Us
slides.content_summary: All models formally rejected; three-factor rejected least (F=1.56) with misfit concentrated in small-growth. Three responses to rejection: multifactor, flawed tests, behavioral. The unifying view: every asset pricing test asks whether some portfolio is MV-efficient — the question is which, and which factors define it.
